summary: Describes an EPP mapping for provisioning and managing Internet host names in a shared central repository, defining command syntax and meaning for hosts. It obsoletes RFC 3732. It is a draft standard, replaced by RFC 5732.

eli5.summary: This note tells how to add or update the name of a server in a registry's book using EPP.

subtitle: Using EPP to manage host objects in a domain registry

tldr.problem: Domain registries need to track host objects (name servers) and allow registrars to provision and manage them. EPP provides the protocol infrastructure, but host objects need their own specific mapping that defines how to create, update, and query host objects in a registry.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4932 defines EPP commands for host objects: check availability, retrieve host details (IP addresses, status), create a new host object with IP addresses, delete a host, and update host attributes (add or remove IP addresses, or change status). Each command uses specific XML elements matching the host namespace.
tldr.outcome: The host mapping enabled registries to manage the name server infrastructure in a standard way. RFC 4932 was later obsoleted by RFC 5732, which refined the mapping and better aligned with DNSSEC and IPv6. Host object provisioning is now standard in modern domain registries.

facts.label: IP Address Versions
facts.value: IPv4 (v4) and IPv6 (v6), with v4 as default

today: RFC 4932 was obsoleted by RFC 5732 in 2009, which refined the protocol and added better DNSSEC and IPv6 support. Host object provisioning in EPP is now the standard for domain registries, with RFC 5732 widely deployed. This RFC documented the intermediate step in EPP's evolution as the de facto standard for domain registry provisioning.

sections.title: Host Objects and Their Role
sections.content:
Host objects in a domain registry represent nameservers and other infrastructure machines. Each host object has a fully qualified name, one or more IP addresses (IPv4 or IPv6), and status values. Host objects have a subordinate relationship to domain objects: a host named "ns1.example.com" is subordinate to the domain "example.com" if both exist in the same registry.

A host can be "internal" (its name is in the registry's name space, such as ns1.example.com in the .example registry) or "external" (its name is outside the registry, such as ns1.otherdomain.net in the .example registry). External hosts are used for delegating to nameservers outside the registry's control. Host objects are created with a set of IP addresses (required only as needed for DNS glue records) and can be updated to add or remove addresses. Host objects cannot be directly transferred; instead, they transfer implicitly when their superordinate domain is transferred.
sections.eli5: A host object is like a phone book entry for a name server. It has the server's domain name and its phone number (IP address). When you own example.com and it uses ns1.example.com as its nameserver, the registry keeps track of ns1.example.com as a separate host object.

sections.title: Host Attributes
sections.content:
Host objects have the following attributes: The fully qualified host name (for example, "ns1.example.com"), which must conform to DNS naming rules (RFC 952 and 1123). IP addresses in both IPv4 (dotted-decimal notation per RFC 791) and IPv6 (colon-hex notation per RFC 4291) formats. Status values that describe the host's state: "ok" for normal operation, "linked" if the host is actively associated with a domain, "clientUpdateProhibited" to prevent modifications, "clientDeleteProhibited" to prevent deletion, or pending statuses for in-progress operations.

Each host object also tracks administrative information: the sponsoring client (who owns it in the registry), the client that created it, creation date, modification dates and the client that last modified it, and the date of the most recent transfer (which occurs when a domain using this host is transferred). Dates are in UTC using ISO 8601 format. Unlike domain objects, host objects do not have explicit authorization information or expiration dates; they persist until deleted or transferred with a domain.
sections.eli5: A host record has the nameserver's name, its IP address (or addresses if it has both IPv4 and IPv6), and notes about whether it's in use or if you can modify it. It also remembers when it was created and who owns it.

sections.title: EPP Host Commands
sections.content:
EPP defines three query commands for host objects: <check> tests whether one or more host names can be provisioned (are they already taken?); <info> retrieves the full details of a host object (IP addresses, status, creation date, modification history); <transfer> has no direct meaning for hosts since transfers happen implicitly when a domain transfers.

EPP defines three transform commands: <create> provisions a new host object with a name and optionally one or more IP addresses; <delete> removes a host object from the registry; <update> modifies host attributes by adding IP addresses, removing IP addresses, changing status, or modifying other properties. <renew> and <transfer> have no meaning for host objects.

A host object should not be deleted while it is actively associated with any domain (linked status). Deleting a host without breaking its associations with domains can cause DNS resolution failures. Subordinate hosts (those in the registry's name space) cannot be deleted if they are still referenced by a domain object in the same registry.
sections.eli5: The commands are: Check (is this nameserver name available?), Info (show me this nameserver's details), Create (add a new nameserver to the registry), Update (change its IP addresses or status), and Delete (remove the nameserver). Transfer doesn't apply to nameservers directly.

sections.title: Command Examples and Responses
sections.content:
A <check> command lists host names to test. The response shows each name with availability (avail="1" if available, avail="0" if taken) and optionally a reason why it is not available. An <info> command retrieves the full details: the host name, assigned ROID (Repository Object Identifier), status values, all associated IP addresses (with versions), sponsoring client, creation information, modification history, and transfer history.

A <create> command specifies the host name and zero or more IP addresses. For hosts used as name servers, addresses are required only to produce DNS glue records; a registrar administering an external nameserver might provision only the name. An <update> command uses add/remove/change operations: add IP addresses, remove IP addresses, or modify status values. A <delete> command removes the host from the registry, and the server responds with an empty response confirming deletion.
sections.eli5: You send XML saying "is ns1.example.com free?", "show me ns1.example.com's details", "create ns1.example.com with IP 192.0.2.1", or "add IPv6 address 2001:db8::1 to ns1.example.com".

sections.title: Internationalization and Server Policies
sections.content:
Host names must conform to RFC 952 (updated by RFC 1123) and can represent internationalized domain names using Punycode (RFC 3490) for non-ASCII characters. IPv4 addresses must conform to RFC 791 notation; IPv6 addresses must conform to RFC 4291. Servers may reject IP addresses that have not been allocated for public use by IANA.

Server operators define policies about which hosts can be created and whether IP addresses are required. When a host is provisioned as a name server for the DNS, addresses are required only as needed to generate glue records. For example, an external nameserver (ns1.otherdomain.net) may not need addresses in the registry. Superordinate domain constraints apply: a subordinate host (like ns1.example.com in the .example registry) cannot be created unless the superordinate domain (example.com) exists in the registry.

Security relies on client authentication through EPP's TLS-based sessions and does not define authorization mechanisms beyond what the base EPP protocol provides. Host objects have no authorization information field like domains do. Server policies determine access to host information and the ability to modify hosts.
sections.eli5: Non-English nameserver names work through Punycode. Servers decide whether you need to provide an IP address (you do if it's a glue record, you don't if it's external). The communication is encrypted and assumes the right people are on both ends.
